transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I guess what finally got me to come in is I keep messing up little things—small stuff, but it adds up. Like at the senior center, I wrote the wrong time on a class sheet, and then people were confused. And the other day I measured a board—just doing a simple little project, nothing fancy—and I still cut it a hair short because I skipped over the small print. I used to be better about that sort of thing, I think. I mean, I’ve always liked doing things with my hands, but these little mistakes are getting frustrating.
Have you been having trouble remembering recent things?

Yeah, sort of. It’s not like I don’t remember anything at all, but my wife will tell me something right to my face—like, “Dave, the cards are in the hall closet now”—and then a minute later I’m standing there thinking, I heard her talking, but I’ve got no idea where she said they were. And then I feel foolish asking again, because she did say it. I was just… I don’t know, not really taking it in.
Have you been feeling down or depressed lately?

I don’t know that I’d say depressed, exactly. I mean, I get frustrated with myself, sure, but “down” like… all the time? I’m not sure. My wife would probably have a better read on it—she notices things before I do, like when I leave the porch light on. But no, I haven’t really been thinking of myself as depressed.
Are you still managing your bills and other finances on your own without mistakes?

Well, the bills… I guess that’s not really the thing I was thinking about when I came in. It’s more these little mistakes that keep catching me, you know? Like at the senior center, I put the wrong time on a class sheet, and then everybody’s asking questions because I’d made it confusing. And I was measuring a board for a little project—something I’ve done plenty of times—and I still cut it just a bit short because I missed the small print. So it’s that kind of thing that’s been bothering me.
Do you need help managing your bills or other finances?

I’m not sure, honestly. My wife knows more about that side of things than I do, because she’ll see the envelopes and remind me, or she’ll say, “Did you take care of that?” But I can’t think of some big mistake with money right now. I mean, bills come in, and then I get sidetracked by the mail pile, or I’ll notice something else in the kitchen and—well, that’s not really what you asked. So… need help? I don’t know that I’d put it that way.
Do you feel like these problems are a real change from how you used to function?

A real change… that’s the part I’m not sure about. I mean, some of it feels more noticeable now, but when I think back, this has kind of been there a long time. Even in elementary school, teachers used to write things like I was bright, but I’d forget my books, lose homework, or just be staring out the window unless somebody kept me on track. My mother saved some of those report cards in a box somewhere—funny what people keep. So, I don’t know if it’s totally new, exactly. It’s more like maybe it’s catching up with me more now.
Before these recent frustrations, did you have the same kinds of attention problems as an adult—like getting sidetracked, losing things, or making careless mistakes?

Well… as an adult, sure, I’ve had bits of that here and there, but the point where it really started getting in the way—where I was noticing it and my wife was noticing it more—was after we moved into the condo. That was about a year and a month ago now, I think.

Moving is funny, you know, you think you’re simplifying, less yard work and all that, but then everything’s in a new place and there are all these little condo rules and papers… Anyway, since then it’s been interfering more noticeably.
Because of these attention or memory problems, do you now need your wife’s help to manage your medications?

Medications… I’m trying to think. I don’t know that I’d say she manages them, exactly. I mean, she’s organized in general—she’ll notice things around the house before I do—but with pills, I’m not sure what counts as “help.” Like, do you mean she reminds me every day, or actually sets them out? I don’t think I’ve really looked at it that way.
Do you need your wife to set up your medications for you?

I don’t know that I’d put it that way. She doesn’t, like, line them all up for me every morning or anything—at least not as a regular thing. We have one of those pill boxes somewhere, actually I think it’s in the kitchen drawer with the batteries, which is probably not the best place for it.

But no, I don’t think I need her to set them up. She might remind me if she notices something, but setting them up for me… I don’t think so.
Do you need your wife’s help to pay the bills?

The bills… my wife’s always been better at keeping an eye on that sort of thing, honestly. I don’t think the bills are the main thing where I’ve needed help, though.

It’s more with plans and keeping things straight. Like I used to help lead a couple of those do-it-yourself workshops—nothing fancy, just at the center—and after a few mix-ups I kind of stepped back from that. My wife has been double-checking plans more, too, so I don’t throw off family visits or things at the center. The bills, I’d have to think about that specifically.
Have you been told by a doctor that you have a brain condition or neurological illness?

I don’t think so… I mean, no doctor has sat me down and said I have a brain condition, as far as I remember. I’ve had regular checkups and all that, and sometimes they use terms I don’t always keep straight, but neurological illness—no, I don’t think anyone’s told me that.

My uncle used to have a whole stack of medical papers on his fridge, which always made me nervous about that kind of thing, but for me, no, I’m not aware of anything like that.
Compared with a year or two ago, have these problems clearly gotten worse?

Yeah… I think so. It’s hard to say exactly, because time kind of runs together for me, but it became more noticeable after we moved into the condo—what was that, about a year and a month ago now.

The move itself was a whole thing, too, with boxes everywhere and figuring out where everything went. I still think some of my tools are in the wrong closet. But since then, yeah, I’d say it’s been interfering more clearly than before.
Because of these problems, have you gotten lost while driving somewhere familiar?

I’m not sure I’d say gotten lost, no. I mean, I’ve taken a wrong turn here or there, but who hasn’t—especially with all the new roadwork near the shopping plaza, they keep moving the cones around and it makes no sense.

But somewhere familiar… I don’t think I’ve actually gotten lost like that. If I’m going someplace I know, I usually get there. Might grumble about the traffic, but I get there.
Because of these problems, do you now need your wife’s help to keep track of appointments?

Yeah, she’s been helping more with that. Not like she’s my secretary or anything, but she’ll double-check the calendar or ask, “Are you sure that’s the right day?” because I’ve mixed up plans a few times.

It’s gotten to where I stepped back from helping lead a couple of those DIY workshops at the center, which bothered me. I used to enjoy showing people little projects—sanding, measuring, that kind of thing. And with family visits too, she kind of checks the plans so I don’t throw everybody off.
Before the move last year, were you having these same kinds of attention problems regularly in your adult life?

Before the move? I mean… I had little things here and there, sure, but I don’t think it was the same kind of regular problem. It really started standing out after we moved into the condo—about a year and a month ago now.

Funny how a move does that, you know, everything gets shuffled around and suddenly you realize you’re not keeping up the way you thought. But yeah, before that, I wouldn’t say it was interfering like it has been since then.
Are you still able to shop for groceries by yourself without getting confused or needing your wife’s help?

Groceries? I can usually do that by myself, yeah. I mean, I might take longer than I used to, especially if they move the cereal aisle around—stores love doing that—but I don’t usually need my wife right there with me.

It’s more the plans and commitments where she’s had to double-check me. Like with family visits, or things at the center, I don’t want to get the time wrong and throw everybody off. That’s part of why I backed off helping lead those DIY workshops, which I still feel kind of bad about.
Do you still cook a meal on your own without making mistakes or needing your wife’s help?

Cooking, uh… mostly I can still make a meal. I haven’t had my wife standing over me or anything. But I do make these little careless mistakes more than I like.

It’s the same sort of thing that brought me in, really—like I’ll write the wrong time on the senior-center class sheet, or I’ll measure a board and still cut it just a bit short because I skipped over some little note or marking. With cooking it’s not usually a disaster, but that kind of “miss the small detail” thing is what gets me.
Has anyone close to you told you that your memory or thinking has clearly gotten worse?

Um… clearly worse? I don’t know that anyone has said it that way to me. My wife will point things out now and then, like if I’m not following what she just told me, but she hasn’t sat me down and said, “Your thinking is getting worse,” if that’s what you mean.

My brother, he’s the type who’d say something blunt if he noticed—actually he once told me my truck sounded like it had “one foot in the grave,” which was rude but he was right—anyway, no, I don’t think anyone close has put it like that.
Has your wife told you that your memory or thinking has gotten worse over the past year?

I don’t think she’s said it like that, no. She’ll remind me about things, but my wife reminds everybody about things—she’s got little notes stuck all over the kitchen, on the fridge, by the coffee maker… actually the coffee maker one has been there so long I don’t even see it anymore.

But, uh, over the past year specifically? I’m not sure she’s told me my memory or thinking has gotten worse. Not in those words, anyway.
Has your wife noticed that your memory or thinking has gotten worse over the past year?

I’m not really sure she’s noticed it like that. I mean, she notices plenty—she notices if the garage light is left on from across the house somehow, and I swear I can walk right past it three times—but as far as my memory or thinking being worse over the past year… I don’t know.

She hasn’t told me that directly. She might say, “I already told you that,” but I don’t know if she means it’s gotten worse or if she’s just annoyed in the moment.

It’s more the plans and commitments where she’s had to double-check me. Like with family visits, or things at the center, I don’t want to get the time wrong and throw everybody off. That’s part of why I backed off helping lead those DIY workshops, which I still feel kind of bad about.

patient.answer:
Cooking, uh… mostly I can still make a meal. I haven’t had my wife standing over me or anything. But I do make these little careless mistakes more than I like.

It’s the same sort of thing that brought me in, really—like I’ll write the wrong time on the senior-center class sheet, or I’ll measure a board and still cut it just a bit short because I skipped over some little note or marking. With cooking it’s not usually a disaster, but that kind of “miss the small detail” thing is what gets me.

doctor.question: Has anyone close to you told you that your memory or thinking has clearly gotten worse?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about whether someone close has noticed a clear worsening in memory or thinking, which is not directly covered by the listed ADHD symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
Um… clearly worse? I don’t know that anyone has said it that way to me. My wife will point things out now and then, like if I’m not following what she just told me, but she hasn’t sat me down and said, “Your thinking is getting worse,” if that’s what you mean.

My brother, he’s the type who’d say something blunt if he noticed—actually he once told me my truck sounded like it had “one foot in the grave,” which was rude but he was right—anyway, no, I don’t think anyone close has put it like that.

doctor.question: Has your wife told you that your memory or thinking has gotten worse over the past year?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about whether his wife has reported a clear worsening in memory or thinking over the past year, which is not directly covered by the listed ADHD symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I don’t think she’s said it like that, no. She’ll remind me about things, but my wife reminds everybody about things—she’s got little notes stuck all over the kitchen, on the fridge, by the coffee maker… actually the coffee maker one has been there so long I don’t even see it anymore.

But, uh, over the past year specifically? I’m not sure she’s told me my memory or thinking has gotten worse. Not in those words, anyway.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is objective corroboration of cognitive decline from an informant, which would help distinguish mild neurocognitive disorder from lifelong ADHD or unspecified cognitive disorder.
doctor.question: Has your wife noticed that your memory or thinking has gotten worse over the past year?

target_item.reason: The question asks whether the wife has noticed worsening memory or thinking over the past year, but the symptom profile does not include an item specifically about collateral observation of cognitive decline.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure she’s noticed it like that. I mean, she notices plenty—she notices if the garage light is left on from across the house somehow, and I swear I can walk right past it three times—but as far as my memory or thinking being worse over the past year… I don’t know.

She hasn’t told me that directly. She might say, “I already told you that,” but I don’t know if she means it’s gotten worse or if she’s just annoyed in the moment.
